utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I am hearing you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic, good morning to you, too. Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think after that, we can have the case called. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Brdjanin and Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose we better hurry and bring the witness in before he starts getting some ideas about applying for Dutch citizenship. Any preliminaries, by the way?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are but I think they probably would be better done after we've finished with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So could you please bring Mr. Dzonlic in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Dzonlic. Sorry about yesterday. It wasn't our fault, as you know. And let's hope nothing happens today which will keep you any further in The Hague. You will hopefully finish with your testimony today, and the gentleman to your right will hand you the usual document on which there is a solemn declaration that you are kindly asked to make.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down, thank you. And Madam Fauveau, before you start, Mr. Ackerman, I take it you still do not take my advice and put that famous question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just believe that I have put the question to him as -- in -- I think I have complied with 90(H)(2). I don't think I am flouting your ruling. I really believe I have complied and that's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment because the witness has got something to tell us. Yes, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise but may I be given my statement again, please? As I was last time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner, can he have the two statements actually? I would suppose it would be wiser to hand both versions to him, both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's been done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzonlic, could you look at your statement dated October, 2000, on page 2. You said that a meeting was held among different Muslim organisations in April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said, during your testimony last week, that this meeting was held because the people were beginning to flee the region of Prijedor, Kozarac and Gradiska. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that people were coming to Banja Luka from those municipalities, which were in the immediate vicinity of Banja Luka. Those who managed to flee had come to Banja Luka or were coming to Banja Luka. I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that this meeting held in April, 1992, was held after the attack on Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were coming after what was happening in Prijedor, Bosanska Gradiska and I think it was also after the attack on Kozarac. I know for sure that these things were happening in Prijedor, Derventa, Bosanska Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I am not asking you about what happened in those places. I am asking you whether that meeting did indeed take place after the attack on Kozarac, as you said last week.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was after the attack on Kozarac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the attack on Kozarac took place?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree if I suggest to you that the attack on Kozarac took place at the end of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't be certain about the dates. I told you that I don't know when the attack on Kozarac took place. If you know for certain, then I -- as I say, I cannot say whether I agree with you or not because I don't know exactly when it took place. But people were coming from Kozarac as well, people were fleeing Kozarac as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that following that meeting, a commission was established to dealt with the rights of prisoners of war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commission was to deal with human rights. The real name of the commission was a Commission for Human Rights and the Implementation of the Geneva Conventions in the Territory of Bosnian Krajina and War Law. But the people, since it dealt most with prisoners, the people referred to it informally as the Commission for Prisoners of War. That's how the people called that commission, by the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Adil Medic was a member of that commission, was he not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know which organisation Adil Medic represented?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a representative of the Forum of Intellectuals, Bosniaks, so he represented the forum of Bosniak intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that he did not represent Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the commission was formed, he did not join it on behalf of Merhamet because on behalf of Merhamet, there was another man who represented Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Adil Medic says that he represented Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Adil Medic said, but my opinion is that when the commission was set up, he joined the commission on behalf of the Forum of Intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at your statement of October, 2000, page 3, please? You said that in March and April, 1992, you went with Adil Medic to the headquarters of the 1st Corps and that two days after this first visit, you met General Talic.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was making this statement, or rather when I saw this statement, when I came here, I did make a few formal, shall I call them objections, regarding this statement, whether it was a lapsus linguae or was it due to the translation, but any way, I said, "Since we went there several times, I don't know exactly who was with me. Sometimes it was Adil Medic, sometimes it was Professor Bajric, sometimes Mr. Halilovic. As far as I can remember, the first time we went there, all four of us were there." So I said that we went there on a number of occasions and because of the number of occasions, I'm not quite sure who was with me on each occasion, whether it was professor -- Mr. Medic, Professor Halilovic, Professor Bajric and myself, or two of us or three of us. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you do still stand by the fact that in April, 1992 you went to the headquarters of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you went there to discuss the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the 1st Corps was established?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but I assume it was just before that, because I know that they told us that it was under the competence of the 1st Krajina Corps. When it was formed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which army that corps belonged to?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It belonged to the Serb army. We called it the Serb army. As far as I know, before it was called the 5th Corps of the JNA, I think, and it was transformed into the 1st Krajina Corps of the Serbian army. We called it the Serbian army. In principle, we called them paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the headquarters of the 1st Corps or to the headquarters of an unknown paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to the headquarters of the 1st Krajina Corps. Naturally, we couldn't tell them that we treat them as paramilitary formations. I know that they told us that this was under the competency of the 1st Krajina Corps, 1st Krajina Corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you treat JNA units also as paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: JNA units were considered by us to be the aggressors, because they were on our territory and Bosnia and Herzegovina was independent, and as foreign troops we treated them as aggressors.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So units of the 1st Corps which you treated as paramilitary units had nothing to do with units of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of formations they were because I'm not a military expert, whether they had anything to do with them or not I don't know. I don't know that. I just know that they were present. That is JNA units were present in those days, and I remember that military judicial institutions started to be formed, the prosecutor's office, the military courts, and I know that members of the JNA assisted quite a bit the people who were in charge of the formation of military institutions of the Serbs; so they assisted in the formation of those institutions. So probably there were links but I cannot comment on those links.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Manjaca camp was set up?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we arrived there, we heard there was talk about that camp. When it was formed, I don't know, but later on, I learnt that people who arrived at the camp first were people from -- now I can't remember the name of a particular village. I think 250 of them who were working there and preparing the area for the arrival of others. So I don't know when that was. But I know that up there at Manjaca there was a military training ground. The largest military tank training ground in the Balkans, it was said to be. And after my university studies, I did some military training there for 15 days, and I know that it existed already.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at page 4 of your statement, still the October, 2000, one, it is the last paragraph. You said that like me, Adil Medic received -- that one month after the meeting, the meeting that according to you took place in April, 1992, you received permission to visit Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we have an accurate reading of that, please? I don't think it says one month. It says about. In the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner is correct, Madam Fauveau. Could you be more specific and perhaps if you have the text in front of you, read the excerpt?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, the witness said [In English] "Prisoners of war decided that we would visit the super military headquarters in Banja Luka. In March or April, 1992, with Imam Alija Halilovic and Adil Medic I attended the military headquarters of the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm very sorry it's my fault. Madam Fauveau, I thought, was reading the passage on page 4, the last paragraph in English, because she was asking the witness about permission to visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's simply the only quarrel I have is that it was stated that the English text reads, "One month later." In fact, it reads, "About one month later."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I said you are correct. Because that's what I had in mine too. Any way, either you rephrase the question, Madam Fauveau, or perhaps you read out those three lines on page 4, the last paragraph, to the witness, who has the text in front of him in any case. I would suggest that you rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that about one month after that meeting with General Talic, Adil Medic received permission to visit the Manjaca camp. Is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, roughly, I couldn't be precise in terms of time. It's very difficult to say. One day we went to our office, that office we had, and as far as I can remember, Adil Medic had been to the headquarters and he came and stated that General Talic had given orders, was it in writing or orally, I don't know, I can't remember. I know that he said that we had been granted permission and that General Talic had issued an order that we could go to Manjaca and that it was our duty to provide identification documents and to take them to the command, and he also gave a date when we should go, that also the date and hour that we would leave in front of the command building. I think it was around 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So, according to you, when you went to see General Talic for the first time, you hadn't been to the Manjaca camp yet?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. We hadn't toured it. We -- between the first time we went and our visit in my judgement, though I find it very hard to fix the time, it was about a month later, because we went there five or six times, certainly. But before that, we hadn't been to Manjaca. It was only after we received permission and after we handed in our -- those documents, and the document of the vehicle that we drove in, only then did we go to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Adil Medic says that there was a meeting with General Talic after the visit to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, as far as I can remember, that when we returned from Manjaca, was it Adil Medic or Professor Bajric, and I think that we wrote a letter in connection with the people that we had agreed should be released from the camp, and I think we addressed that letter to the command as a notification, either we asked for their release or we wrote a letter saying that it had been agreed that they be released, and there were contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I'll come to that a little later but for the moment, I'm saying that Adil Medic says that he visited Manjaca because Adil Medic contacted Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but in our submission, it's not a proper way to cross-examine to say, "Did you know that Adil Medic said this?" That's a matter of comment on which you can be address. The witness can be asked if he is sure that that's what happened and if he adheres to it fine, if he doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand, Ms. Korner, you are right. On the other hand, I can't blame Madam Fauveau that much. Perhaps you will take what I'm going to tell you in the spirit that I am saying it. Basically, what Madam Korner -- what Madam Korner is saying is that kind of question that you should put to him, if we are to follow the basic rules of a proper cross-examination, is not to ask the witness whether -- if he knows what another witness has stated, either here or outside the courtroom. But to put it to him as a possibility or as an affirmation, and then ask him, either for his comment or whether he agrees that this happened or whatever. I mean, in your case, I was going to stop you for another reason because the way you put the question is sort of -- you were hinting to the witness that in saying that they met General Talic before visiting Manjaca, he was not being precise and that another witness had said that they met General Talic after visiting Manjaca. In actual fact, I -- this is why I'm mentioning it, perhaps you could be very specific. You just tell the witness what you believe Adil Medic stated, and then ask him whether he agrees or disagrees, but you don't ask him what the other witness stated. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Adil Medic said [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] General Talic called the Mufti Alija Halilovic and told him that humanitarian aid was possible to issue to the prisoners of Manjaca. Talic inquired if it was possible to arrange this." Do you know whether General Talic called the mufti Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether General Talic called the late mufti in Banja Luka but I do know that the mufti had a meeting with General Talic too, but I don't know when exactly. The late mufti had a meeting not only with General Talic but also with the entire leadership at that time, on several occasions, but whether he called him or not, this is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: After the visit to Manjaca, did you go to meet General Talic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the visit to Manjaca, I had the most contact with international representatives and our office would go to the command, but I don't know who they would meet. All I can say is that I remember that after we returned from Manjaca we wrote to the command. I don't know whether it was to inform them that such and such a number of people would leave or whether it was to request that a certain number of people leave. I can't state this precisely now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: After the first visit to Manjaca, were you present at a meeting with General Talic or not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After I returned from Manjaca, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this request for release that you wrote. Could you tell us what it was, this request?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I wrote it. I think that Mr. Adil Medic wrote it and as I say, I know that a request was written when we came back from Manjaca. Whether it was to inform the command that it was necessary to release a certain -- certain people in certain categories, or whether the request was that we had agreed in Manjaca, at Manjaca, that a certain number of people would be released, and that we had agreed to this in Manjaca, the request was something like this, but I didn't write it. It was written by Adil Medic on behalf of the office, and I wrote a report and certain requests for the International Red Cross and the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you met General Talic the first time, did he speak to you about the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the camp was a camp for war prisoners and that it was under the authority of the 1st Krajina Corps, and that everything with regard to the camp -- that these people were responsible for everything in the camp, the people who were present there. It's possible that he said that everything was in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, that the prisoners were being treated in accordance with these conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar show the witness document DT2? It is 41586.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, is this a new exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have it either. I don't recall having ever seen it, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I gave it to the Registrar on last Friday with a list of documents that I was going to use.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps while that document is being looked for, could I ask -- I'm not clear whether the suggestion to the witness is that he is wrong when he says the meeting with General Talic was before the visit to Manjaca. If that's the case, I think that ought to be put. He's been cross-examined about what Mr. Dzonlic said but is the case that he when he said the meeting was before is wrong or that Mr. Dzonlic was wrong. That's the trouble with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why earlier on you may have noticed I said, I told Ms. Fauveau I was on the point of stopping her. But I think it has been more or less cleared now, and that she does acknowledge that there were two meetings, one before and one after, and she's got it from the witness that while he was present at the first meeting he was not present at the second one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ah, well, Your Honour, in that case Your Honour has certainly followed it more clearly than I have, if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree, Madam Fauveau, with what I have just stated? I think she put a very direct question to the witness when he avoided answering the question that she had just put to him, whether he was present at the second meeting, at the meeting which took place after the visit to Manjaca and he didn't answer that question. Whether he avoided purposely to answer that question, I don't know, but he did not answer that question, so she put the question in a more direct fashion immediately afterwards. And he answered that he was not present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I wonder if -- can I just be clear myself? That is the suggestion: Two meetings, but Mr. Dzonlic wasn't present at the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can go through the transcript. Let me change my glasses.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right with regard to the interpretation of what the witness said, but I don't quite agree with what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's another matter. That you don't agree with what he said is another matter, but that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... direct and specific question to him. And in fact your next question was with reference to what you referred to as the first meeting. For him, there was only one meeting. There wasn't a first and a second. For you, there were two meetings. For us there were two meetings because basically we know there was a second meeting at which you have referred, at least from the evidence of someone else. But he stated that he was not present at the second meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think this is where the problem has arisen and I think it's because -- I don't for one moment blame Madam Fauveau, it's because of the style of putting the questions. My understanding rather was that there was only one meeting and that took place after the visit to Manjaca, ergo this witness is wrong. That's what I understand the suggestion to be, but it was quite difficult to follow and if that is the suggestion, I think it should be put in plain terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, Madam Fauveau, let's be very clear. Are you suggesting to the witness that there were two meetings or just one meeting and that one meeting took place after the visit to Manjaca and not before?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am suggesting that there was one meeting after the visit to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that is the question that is obviously being put to you again, Mr. Dzonlic. Is it possible that there was only one meeting with Mr. Talic at which you were present, and that meeting took place after the visit to Manjaca and not before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was at a meeting before we went to Manjaca, and after Manjaca, I wasn't present at any other meeting after Manjaca. I know that they went to the command after Manjaca, but as for a meeting, I don't know, but I do know -- but as I said, I don't know -- I went for sure on three or five -- three, four, five times. I went there before we went to Manjaca. And on one occasion, and this was before we went to Manjaca, not after Manjaca, as far as I can remember. I don't know. I didn't have a meeting with General Talic after Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting that you attended before visiting Manjaca, was Adil Medic present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it's written down here. I can't exactly remember who was there because we went there on several occasions. We went there very often. I even know that we sometimes had to go to the command two or three times in the course of one day. We would go there two or three times in order to establish contact. I don't exactly know who was with me at the meeting, whether Adil Medic was there. In my statement, it states that -- and I thought that this was perhaps an error, maybe when I was speaking of when it was translated, but we had a meeting before going to Manjaca before going to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you went to the headquarters of the 1st Corps on several occasions. Did you see General Talic on each occasion?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on each occasion. I saw him one other time when I was passing -- he passed by. I saw him one other time. As I said, we went there quite often. But the second time that I saw him, we didn't speak to each other. I only saw him over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you only had one meeting with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you don't remember whether Adil Medic was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I can't remember. I sometimes went there on my own and sometimes the two of us went there. Sometimes Adil Medic went on his own. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Dzonlic, I'm not speaking about visits to the headquarters. I'm only speaking about the meeting with General Talic, the one meeting.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was with you at this meeting with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know exactly who was with me. I don't know whether Adil Medic was there or Professor Bajric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, I suggest you move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, do you have an order from General Talic in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read the last paragraph, the third paragraph? Could you read it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read it out loud, please?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To prisoners of war, behave with dignity, treat them in a humane way. Do not subject them to violence, insult them or frighten them. Make sure that they have accommodation and provide those who are sick with medical care, in accordance with international war law."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, slow down, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'd like to inform you that the interpreters do not have this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And another problem is that apparently this document has not been copied -- has not been handed to the interpreters. So if the Registry perhaps could remedy that, if there are spare copies. Are you going to put further questions on this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, which concerns the document but it's not necessary for him to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You don't have any further copies, but are there any other documents because this unfortunately we were not updated on this matter. Are there any other documents, DT documents, which are going to be made use of by Madam Fauveau this morning or later on in the course of her cross-examination of witnesses? Because if that is the case, perhaps while she goes along we have them photocopied so we have copies -- the Prosecution I understand have copies already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were given copies last week. It's actually one of our documents and I think it's probably already got a "P" number, but that's going to happen quite a lot, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could have someone here who can have them photocopied, at least for the interpreters, because I understand we will be given our copy as we go along. Thank you. Sorry to have interrupted you like that, Madam Fauveau, but I think it was necessary. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, do you agree that in this order, General Talic requested that prisoners of war be treated in accordance with the rules of the rights of war law?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to the Manjaca camp, you went in a red van; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this van belonged to -- to Ibrahim Makic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was his van.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Makic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Mr. Makic. I think he worked as a representative of Merhamet. I think that was in Vrbanja. I don't know who Mr. Makic is. I didn't know him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Adil -- was Adil Medic present at this visit to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at the moment, I need to show the witness another document and I assure you that I gave it to the Registrar last Friday. It is P467 but in the original form, without the notes that the previous witness provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, could you show us where the entrance to the Manjaca camp is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's follow the usual procedure here. As you show us Mr. Dzonlic, please you're going to be handed a coloured pen and please mark. For example, if you're going to show us where the entrance is, you mark it on the document itself, and put your initials against it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] [Interpretation] According to this drawing, in my opinion, the entrance is here, the entrance to the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, it is where you've put an "X" inside a circle? Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in the camp of Manjaca, you did visit the stables?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did but only to this -- this one and this one, but we didn't go to this one up here. We weren't able to enter it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark with an "X" the two stables that you did visit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not with an "X," with a number "1," "2," however -- whatever the number was, of the -- of what is being referred to as stables that you visited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] [Interpretation] We entered these two.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony on the 27th of February, you said that the camp was surrounded by a double barbed wire fence. Could you indicate on this drawing where that fence is?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this drawing, as far as I can see, there is only one fence. This is one fence that has been drawn, that I had in mind, when I said that the camp was fenced in inside, because these stables and this kitchen where the detainees were, there was this fence round it, but there is another fence that can't be seen on this drawing, which surrounds the whole camp. So these stables and the kitchen where the detainees were held had a fence of the kind drawn, but there was also another fence around the camp as a whole but I don't see it on the drawing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So this drawing doesn't show us the whole camp; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see the whole camp, yes, because at the entrance, somewhere around here, there are some additional premises, as far as I can find my way on this drawing, because we entered into some other buildings, sheds.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said on the 27th of February, and I quote, "Actually, around each of these three stables, there was also a barbed wire."

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been a slip. I didn't say around each of the stables but around these three stables and this building where they ate. There was a fence, not around each and -- each stable, but all of them together had this fence around them, precisely in the way it is indicated on this drawing, rather than each of the stables individually having a fence around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 7 of your statement of October, 2000, in the Serbo-Croatian version, it is page 6, you said that you asked for permission to speak to the detainees and that your request was turned down. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said to us that we could not -- no, we didn't ask, but when we talked to them, they told us that we couldn't talk to the detainees, that's what they told us. Before we entered those stables, at a meeting that we held when we entered the camp, we were told that we could not talk to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you visited these stables, was Adil Medic with you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All four of us toured the stables. We visited them together, together, not just the stables but the whole camp. They showed it to us, and as far as I can remember, all four of us toured it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Adil Medic was able to speak to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I too managed to speak to detainees during the tour, and it's quite possible that Adil Medic spoke to them as well as Professor Bajric may have done. Though we knew we had been told that we couldn't talk to the detainees, nonetheless, walking through those stables and among the detainees, we did talk to them regardless of the order given to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke to the detainees, were the guards present?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a feeling that there was a soldier or a guard or a -- escorting each one of us and they were always present throughout the time we spent in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So when you managed to speak to the detainees, someone was always present?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were never without an escort.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to suggest to you that Adil Medic was able to speak to the detainees in a way that the guards would not hear it, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree. We were under observation. I don't know. They were present next to us all the time, and I think there was one guard next to each one of us. In fact, there may have been more than four of them. We were four, but there may have been more than four of them. So I don't know. They saw us talking, and when I was speaking, they could see that we were communicating. They were right behind us in our immediate vicinity. So I -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony last week, you said that most of the detainees in the stables were lying down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them were lying down, most of them, the majority. Compared to what I saw in the pictures here, when all of them were sitting, when we were there in my opinion, most of them were lying down. There were some sitting down, some standing, but there were many lying down. Now, whether it is a majority or not, I think that many of them were lying down.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I suggest to you that all the detainees were standing except for one single one, who was lying down, you wouldn't agree with me?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, this statement is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you visit the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That time, once when we toured the camp, and I went on one other occasion, though I didn't enter the camp itself. After sometime, I can't tell you exactly after how long, when we went parcels to the camp, I went once with the truck delivering the packages but I didn't enter the camp. We stopped outside the entrance to the camp. On that occasion, I didn't enter or tour the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Merhamet regularly deliver aid to the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember immediately after our return from the camp, aid was sent in a truck. Merhamet purchased some cabbage, I think, potatoes, onions, and I think that this was sent, and as far as I'm able to remember, maybe on one other occasion, food was sent by truck in this way. However, after that, it was agreed and permitted for individual packages to be addressed to a particular person by name. So I cannot remember, and I'm unable to say how often this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that between June and December, 1992, Merhamet delivered aid to the Manjaca camp 49 times?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I told you that after returning from the camp, I focused more on activities with the International Red Cross. So I don't know how many times Merhamet did, and whether that is possible, but I do know that after we returned, it was agreed that eight days later the International Red Cross would come. However, it took perhaps more than a month, and it was only then that the International Red Cross came, and I think that the International Red Cross assisted in providing humanitarian aid to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I'm not challenging the aid of the International Red Cross, but in addition to the International Red Cross, could Merhamet have delivered humanitarian aid to the Manjaca camp 49 times?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I don't know that, I think. I don't remember, or rather I can't say. I told you what I know, that perhaps a truck went twice, and it carried food in bulk, loose, and after sometime, it also delivered some packages, and I went once when these packages were being Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. delivered. But I don't know how many times. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the release of certain persons in July from Manjaca. After that release, were there other releases in August or September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were some then too, I think on one other occasion, as far as I can remember, another group of people. Now, whether it was August or September, I don't know, but as far as I can remember, there was another group of people released.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In August, you had regular contacts with the Red Cross, did you not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was constantly in touch with the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to suggest to you that in August, a group of prisoners were released and sent through the intermediary of the Red Cross to Western Europe, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that a group was sent when the camp was closed, through the International Red Cross, to a collection centre in Karlovac. As far as I know. I don't know that a certain group, through the Red Cross was sent in August. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of a group of prisoners being sent through the mediation of the Red Cross for medical treatment to Switzerland and Great Britain?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a certain number of religious officials were released from Manjaca in September?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they were release after our visit, that religious officials were released, but as for a group in the month of September, don't know. But I assume that there were religious officials as well, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that some religious officials were released after your visit and you allow for the possibility that others may have been released in September. Is my understanding of what you said right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a -- I was saying this second time when they were released, I know that a certain group of people, I remember that this group was released. I don't know which category they were. But in view of the fact that after our visit there were religious officials in the group, I know that they kept insisting that religious officials should be released and so it's possible that there were religious officials in that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Manjaca camp was closed?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in -- at the end of 1992, maybe in December or November. I don't know the exact date. I can't say. But I think it was towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that simultaneously with the release of prisoners from the Manjaca camp, Serb prisoners should have been released from Croat and Muslim camps?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1992, you were still in contact with the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the International Red Cross was involved in the release of prisoners from the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was under their patronage. They organised the closing of the camp, and the transfer of people in the direction of Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: What were your relations with Merhamet in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any relations with Merhamet. I was a member of the executive board of the SDA for Banja Luka and this body was set up, as I described earlier on, for the protection of human rights, under the patronage of Merhamet, so on behalf of Merhamet. However, I had no relations with Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the SDA have relations with Merhamet in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the associations of Bosniaks had relations with it, but each did its part of the work, the SDA, the political activities; Merhamet, humanitarian; Preporod, cultural; the Islamic Community, religious. But there was no intermingling or interference in the affairs of each other's but there was a relationship among them being Bosniak institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I shall move on to another subject. Could the registry give the witness Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to draw your attention, Madam Fauveau, that we will be having a break very soon. So if you think that within the next five minutes, you can put the next few questions and close a particular segment of your cross-examination, yes, go ahead. If you think you're going to open a new chapter, then perhaps we could break now and resume in half an hour's time. Tell me what you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer to have the break now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a short break of about 25 minutes, resuming at ten to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime -- [Microphone not activated] Yes. The witness is here. Madam Fauveau, please proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before continuing my cross-examination, I would like to request that the document that was shown to the witness, and which is marked P -- it's the drawing of Manjaca. I would like it to be designated as DT3 because it's a new document and it has been marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's granted. And we may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar provide the witness with the Prosecutor's document DT7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's DT7, it's not a Prosecution's document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a document which you have seen already.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, this is the Official Gazette of the Region of Krajina, which you have already seen. Could you have a look at the first decision, the very first one, which has been signed by Milorad Sajic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I can't find it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the very first page, the very first page of this document, if you have the right document before you, it's P227, contains a decision of the Secretariat for National Defence of the ARK, of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, dated 4th May, 1992, and signed, as suggested to you, by Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Sajic. Has he got the right document?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, do you now have the decision signed by Milorad Sajic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing last week, you said that you didn't know who Milorad Sajic was but that you did know that he had connections with the army; do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that he signed this decision as secretary of the Regional Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this organ, the National Defence Secretariat, is not a military organ but an organ which is attached to the civilian government?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about Nikola Erceg. You said that he was the president of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Executive Council of Krajina, of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you specify which executive council you were talking about, of the assembly or of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region. That was in fact the government, the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you do agree that the Autonomous Region of Krajina had an assembly and this assembly had a government which was called the executive committee?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing on the 1st of March, you mentioned regions and you also mentioned the region of Banja Luka, Bihac and Tuzla. You said that these regions were not -- did not belong to a legal category; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They were, so to speak, historical regions, which had been treated by the people as such. They would speak of the Tuzla area or the Tuzla basin, the Banja Luka area, the Bihac and Sarajevo area, the Mostar area, but they weren't in -- they didn't constitute a constitutional category. It was an economic and industrial category, if we are speaking about the regions in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that before 1990, Banja Luka, Bihac and Tuzla were centres of the association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They weren't centres of the association of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want to say that before 1990, there was no association of the municipalities of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, an association of municipalities of Banja Luka did not exist. As far as I can remember, there was no such association of municipalities of Banja Luka or of the municipalities of Bihac, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, however, that the association of municipalities was a legal category in constitutional terms too? At least?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the association of municipalities in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, which were municipalities in the sense of municipalities which were self-managing, I think there was something but I can't be explicit about this with regard to the municipalities, at the level of local administration and self-management, but I don't know if there were any associations of municipalities in these regions. But as far as I can remember, Bosnia had 104 municipalities and all these municipalities formed an association of municipalities as an association of municipalities so to speak, which -- whose task was to develop local administration and self-management. That's what I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I said that they were related to the -- association of municipalities in accordance with the Yugoslav constitution, you wouldn't agree with me?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree if you are thinking of the association of municipalities within these autonomous regions. I wouldn't agree with that. I know an association of municipalities but whether it was called the association of municipalities or community of municipalities and this was at the level of the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was not at the level of the Autonomous Region, not at the level of the Autonomous Region for sure, because the constitution didn't provide for any sort of autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I suggest that Bosnia was divided into seven associations of municipalities, you wouldn't agree with that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, may I ask you to be more specific within a specific time frame because your question initially referred to 1990. Are you still in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am still talking about the period concerned, before 1990, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm going to move on to another subject in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 26th of February, 2002, you said that you had found out who was the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, one moment, Madam Fauveau. There is a further point that we would like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and clarify for the Chamber and give us the specific provision of the constitution you were just elaborating on concerning the municipalities? And please do it because you touch constitutional level very often, give us always the provision because otherwise we cannot really know where are you going. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President and Your Honours, I have forwarded all the constitutions that are concerned, that of Yugoslavia and Bosnia to the translation service and as soon as I have the translations I have provide you with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we can probably assist. I think somewhere in the bowels of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Ms. Korner, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we may be able to assist. I think we do have a translated copy somewhere of the constitution and we will have a look. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Any way, if you explore a certain provision, you yourself must know that provision so I think it would help to everybody if you could mention that provision. I'm sure -- I know a lot of constitutions so those provisions are very, very simple. They are not long.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Yugoslav constitution unfortunately is not at all simple. It had more than 400 articles and that is the case for the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina too and as this is not an expert in constitutional matters, as I'm not an expert in constitutional matters, I don't -- I can't say this by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I didn't ask for opinion, but if you touch certain provision, you can read that provision. I don't want you to read the whole parts of the constitution but that certain provision.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me to do so, the witness, Mr. Donia, referred to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is being asked actually of you, Madam Fauveau, is very simple. You have suggested to the witness that there may have been already in place in 1990 a system of association of municipalities, which had, as its source, legal source, the constitution, as I understood you, the constitution of the Republic of Yugoslavia, and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and also the constitution of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what Judge Janu is suggesting to you, and she is right, that properly speaking when you address such a subject, such a particular area, in putting a question to the witness, who I understand is not an expert in constitutional law like you are not an expert in constitutional law, you should identify to him the relevant part of the constitution, say if it's section -- article 210, you would say, "Are you aware that in terms of article 210 of the former republic -- the constitution of the former Republic of Yugoslavia there were provisions already in place for associations of municipalities?" Not just in Bosnia and Herzegovina presumably but also in other regions. I don't know because I have never studied the constitution of the former Republic of Yugoslavia. If you don't have it now we will make up for it later on but take it as the normal practice for the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do so in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the hearing of the 26th of February, 2002, you said that you had learned who the president of the Crisis Staff was through the decision that you had seen and which had been signed by this president, and you also said that you had heard who the president of the Crisis Staff was; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the other members of the Crisis Staff were?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who the other members of the Crisis Staff were?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we could see in the decision which I have here, on the second page, this can be seen, and as far as I remember, this has already been asked of me. I have already been asked whether I knew certain people from that Crisis Staff, people whom I had identified and I said that I knew certain details about some of them. I don't know all the people in the Crisis Staff, but the ones I have heard about, I have mentioned these people. I have said what I know about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Indeed, Madam Fauveau, what he has just affirmed now is correct. He was asked this question, not by you admittedly but he was asked this question and with reference to practically all the members of the Crisis Staff as they appear on page 3 of Exhibit P227. So if we could move to your next question, it would be better.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but the witness said at the hearing of the 26th of February that he had learnt who the president was because he had been told, and thanks to reading the decision from the Crisis Staff. He never referred to the decision that he saw here, the decision according to which the members of the Crisis Staff -- naming the members of the Crisis Staff. And what I'm interested in is whether he had seen this decision at that time, that is to say in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the question is, Mr. Dzonlic, had you seen this decision that you have in front of you, or anything like it, at the relevant time, that is, in May, 1992, or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't see it. And as far as I can remember, I didn't say that I had seen it at the time. I never stated such a thing, as far as I can remember now. I didn't see that decision because I saw it here. The first time I saw the decision was now. I mean not now, but in the course of the investigation, and I was surprised when I saw, as far as I can remember, this is what I stated, I didn't know that some of the people whom I knew were members of the Crisis Staff, but in 1992, I knew that the president of the Crisis Staff was Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. This is something that I did know because this was a well-known fact in the city but I hadn't seen the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the persons for whom you know that they were members of the Crisis Staff in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Radoslav Brdjanin was the president of the Crisis Staff. This I knew. But as far as the other people are concerned, I didn't know that they were members of the Crisis Staff. I only knew that Radoslav Brdjanin was the president because this is what was said in town, there were stories that he was the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard -- did you ever hear in 1992 that General Talic was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I knew that he was the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps but I never heard that he was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 26th of February, you said that the official newspapers were sent to all those -- all the budget beneficiaries; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the Official Gazettes would be sent to -- that they should be sent and were sent to all budget beneficiaries, and to economic -- to public institutions, to companies, to socially owned companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that certain institutions were budget beneficiaries, beneficiaries of the municipal budget and others were beneficiaries of the republican budget?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should be. Yes, I agree that some of them were beneficiaries at the municipal level and others at the republican level, or rather -- yes, I agree that some institutions should be -- although in Banja Luka, there weren't republican institutions and when I say that, I'm thinking -- I'm referring to the institutions of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know whether there were institutions of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: A beneficiary of the republican budget, would he have also received the Official Gazette of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I assume that such a beneficiary should receive it. But as that was a higher level body, then the lower level, the municipality body, would not be obliged to do that, but by way of information, he should receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So in Bosnia, the institutions that were beneficiaries of the republican budget would receive the Official Gazette of the republic. And the Official Gazettes of 104 municipalities, what about those?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that as far as I am able to remember now, the question was who received the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and I said that the recipients should have been those who benefited from the budget of the Autonomous Region. And the municipal Official Gazette should have been received by beneficiaries of the municipal budget, and institutions, public institutions, enterprises that were state-owned, that most of the capital came from the state, so they should have received the municipal Official Gazettes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the army an institution that benefited from the budget of the republic? That was financed out of the republican budget?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which republic budget you are now referring to. Are you referring to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? If you're referring to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the legal army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was financed out of the budget of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know which republic budget you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did use the budget of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina receive the Official Gazettes of the municipalities which were a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I doubt that the army received the municipal Official Gazette. I don't know, but I doubt that the army received it, the municipal gazette, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree in that case that the Army of Republika Srpska also received the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska and not the Official Gazettes of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I object to that question. How can he answer that? He wasn't part of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you in a position to answer that question, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, are you in a position to answer that question, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you possibly know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just -- I think I could just express an opinion of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need opinions. It's -- the whole question is you are being asked a question, whether you are in a position to answer it or not. And that's what we want to know, whether you could have possibly been in information which would have put you in a position to answer it. If you don't know, just say, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it. So we will move to something else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the hearing on the 28th of February, you said that you were not aware of the expression "state of war," or "imminent threat of war."

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember now. Could you perhaps remind me of that? That I said that I didn't know of the expression "state of war," or "immediate threat of war"? Maybe, as far as I can remember, when I was asked in connection with the Crisis Staff, I said that as far as I remembered and as far as I knew, the Crisis Staff was provided for by the law in emergencies such as floods, fires, earthquakes, natural disasters, but that I didn't know it was envisaged for a time of war or immediate threat of war. If that is what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have the transcript, Madam Fauveau, would you just read the excerpt to him, to the witness, because I think you are talking at cross-purposes here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was -- did we speak before of another text? That was the question by Ms. Korner. And the answer was, "We didn't talk about war. We spoke about natural disasters, earthquakes, floods, et cetera. We didn't speak of a state of war but of emergencies."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question to the witness is whether, in other texts, he saw this expression?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I just have the page number reference? In the LiveNote, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 2474, Livenote.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, could you answer that question? Have you seen in any Yugoslav text this expression being used?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that as far as I knew, the notion of a Crisis Staff applied to what I said before, to these extraordinary situations, emergencies, and I think that it was regulated by the law on civil defence. That's what I think. And as far as I can remember, there was the law on civil defence. I don't know of any other document or act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Dzonlic. The question that you are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. being asked is a very simple, straightforward one. You are not being asked to explain what, in your opinion, should have been or ought to have been the rationale of a Crisis Staff. You are being asked sicate simpliciter a very simple question: Did you at any time during the period in question, ever see a document in which the phrase "state of war or imminent or immediate threat of war" appeared or featured? Obviously in relation to the constitution or the setting up of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to suggest to you that Article 317 of the Yugoslav constitution confers to executive body's special rights in a state of war or in a state of imminent threat of war, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you have seen that expression elsewhere before?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen it but if you say that it is Article 318 or 19, whatever you said, of the constitution, then I -- I don't remember seeing it, but if it is an article of the constitution, then I would agree with you. Perhaps at some point in time earlier on I did see it while I was a student, while I was at the university, but I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- full faith in you and your knowledge of the Yugoslav constitution, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, the difficulty is that if it hadn't been clarified the way the question is phrased, "Would you agree with me?" I think, so we all understand what the witness is saying, it should be phrased, "Have you ever seen article?" because otherwise when we come back to read the transcript and it hasn't been clarified, we are going to have terrible problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But as a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead. Maybe you can send Mr. Dzonlic back home. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm concerned about the interpreters so I was listening.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the hearing of the 27th of February this year, you said that the SDA took the decision not to take part in the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka at a given point in time. Could you tell us what time of year this was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be specific about when this happened, but I do know that such a decision was taken, and I noticed that when I was - during the investigation and during my testimony - referring to dates, that I had problems with dates, because it was a long time ago, so I don't know when this was but I do know that we took the decision to withdraw, to pull out of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could it have been in April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I said that I didn't know. So I can't give you a date. I can't tell you when it was. There were many events, numerous developments so it is very difficult. I simply can't say whether it is possible that it was in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that that decision was also taken or a similar decision was taken by the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the HDZ also -- I'm not aware of their decision, but I do know that there were negotiations with the HDZ and that they also supported this decision and that they also withdrew from the parliament, so they probably took a decision to that effect. So I -- but I do know that they withdrew from the parliament and that there were interparty negotiations. I took part in them sometimes, but there were daily negotiations and discussions as to whether I was present when that joint decision was made, I don't know, but I do know that they also withdrew from the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the president of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Nikola Gabelic, I think his name was, Nikola Gabelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Gabelic continued to attend municipal assembly sessions of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
