utterances.text: I don't know whether he continued to attend sessions. I am of the opinion, what is more, that he was not a municipal deputy, as far as I know. I know he was president of the HDZ for Banja Luka but I'm not sure that he was a member of the municipal assembly. He may have been. I don't know. I just do know that he was president of the HDZ for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registry show the witness DB32B, Brdjanin Defence document?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's an exhibit whose pages have not been numbered unfortunately, so Mr. Dzonlic, if you could look from the back of the document, and find the eighth page from the back?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid that the witness has not found the right page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've managed to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a page with three signatures?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the English version be placed on the ELMO for the interpreters, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please put the English version on the ELMO so that the interpreters can follow?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid the witness still hasn't found the right page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, could you show the usher the page you are referring to so that he can then direct the witness accordingly, please? The page where there are the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, would you agree that at the very bottom of the page, there is a certification of Nikola Gabelic as being a member of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this testifies to the presence of Nikola Gabelic at a meeting of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka held on the 16th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So Nikola Gabelic, the president of the HDZ, did indeed attend meetings of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka in October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the hearing on the 27th of February, you said that more than 50.000 Bosniaks and more than 30.000 Croats left Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And during the hearing of the 1st of March, you said there were 28.700 Bosniaks in Banja Luka. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain, then, how 50.000 Bosniaks could have left Banja Luka when there was a total of 28.700 of them in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain. I worked, as I have already said, on the census of 1981 and the census of 1991. As far as I am able to remember now, at the last census, in addition to Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs, there were Yugoslavs and there were "others". While I was working as a census taker in the census commission, I would meet a large number of people who, by first and last names, or only by one of the two, that is by first or last name, were in fact Muslims, that is Bosniaks, so that, as far as I can remember, when a referendum was held, the referendum for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the basis of the listings of all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we assigned people to count among all those Yugoslavs who declared themselves as Yugoslavs and who, judging by the name, that is the first and last name and the name of their father, and I remember that perhaps out of 23.000 -- sorry, 2.000 or 3.000.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there were about, out of the 23.000, there were 20.000 Muslims. So it was on that basis that I made that statement. Because we treated those people as Muslims. And they declared themselves as Yugoslavs because Yugoslavia was our state, and as far as I know, the concept of a Yugoslav nation never existed, but you see, everyone was allowed to declare themselves as they wished, in terms of ethnicity, so they could also declare themselves as Yugoslavs, but judging by their names and surnames and father's names, we established that in Banja Luka there were more than 50.000 Muslims, members of the Islamic faith, and it was on that basis that I said that close to 50.000 Bosniaks and close to 30.000 Croats had been expelled from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, when there were elections in Banja Luka, there were leftist parties, the reformists and the SDP party. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I wouldn't quite agree entirely, because the SDP was a leftist party, whereas the reformists, I wouldn't call them a leftist party, but rather an idea of reformism.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among the candidates at the elections on the list of these parties, there were people of all nationalities, were there not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar give the witness Exhibi -- Brdjanin Defence document DB31B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just ask where we are going on this, and what the relevance of this is to the Defence case for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Ms. Korner accepts the cross-examination I did of the witness, I don't remember his number, then I will not engage in this exercise. I'm sure Ms. Korner knows the number of the witness. If not, it has to do with the credibility of the witness and the number of Muslims in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have not really understood you. Would you repeat or rephrase what you said? I mean, the question that Ms. Korner has just put or the remark, in other words, she would like to know where you're heading and why you are asking this sequence of questions, having already had a statement from -- or a reply from the witness explaining why, according to him, the number of Bosniaks or Muslims was not just the 28.000 whatever but also another 20-odd thousand from the rest who had declared themselves to be as Yugoslavs, so where are you heading now?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we can't accept that among the 20.000 Yugoslavs there were 20.000 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay. Go ahead but please keep it within acceptable, because although he used to work in the census department, I do not consider him the spokesman for the census department, so let's see what this document has to tell us, anyway. As usual, Mr. Usher, please to the witness you give the version in B/C/S and on the ELMO, please put the English version so that the interpreters can follow. Yes, your question, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before pursuing the matter, Mr. President, I'm referring to the second witness who put forward this thesis, if the Prosecutor asked this question each time during the examination, then I think that this is relevant to the case. So -- as we are obliged to contest everything, I prefer to contest this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, could you have a look at page 5, the list of candidates, the list of reformist candidates?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we don't have the English version on the ELMO yet. It should be easier in the English version. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The translators, I believe, do have this document, if that's what your concern is, Your Honour. We certainly gave it to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Interpreters, do you have this document handy?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, once more, you're wrong. They don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this is the document, I have a vague recollection, but without the name of the witness that was put, which shows that some of the names of people calling themselves Yugoslavs are clearly not Muslim names, then I'm not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it's that document. I think it's another document which purports or gives us lists of members or candidates for the different parties. I don't recall the names, remember the names but it's a different document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. But it is the one that shows that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people were calling themselves Yugoslavs with obviously not Bosniak names.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I accept that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we can go ahead, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has still got to answer that question. Have you found the page? Usher, can you bring me that document here, please? Here. What we need is from part 4, this part of the page, and then crosses over to the other page. Do you want, Madam Fauveau, the first part of the first nine names? Because in the English version, they are partly, very few, on page -- on one page, and the -- on page 4, and the bulk is on page 5. If you are going to ask direct questions to the witness with reference to someone in particular, then please tell me whether it's the first nine or the bulk from ten to 116 or then the end, remaining from 117 to 129.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first name is under number 6 but I don't know if it would be useful to proceed with this series of questions, given what Ms. Korner has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But you don't have a confirmation from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I will ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, do you have the list of candidates of the Reformist Party in front of you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see whether, among these persons, these candidates, can you see whether there are any Yugoslavs among them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a look at the person under number 19, Spasoje Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this person a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at number 22, would you agree with me that this person is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The person under number 28, is that person a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The persons under number 30 and 31, they are Muslims, you would agree?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with regard to number 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 31 is not a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- I suggest to you, Madam Fauveau, that we could stop here with regard to this list, and move ahead. If that is agreeable to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, would you agree that the choice of nationality is a matter of personal conviction?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, why did you take the liberty of treating Bosniaks, people who had declared themselves to be of Yugoslav nationality, why did you take the liberty to declare them as Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't declare them to be Bosniaks. We considered them to be Muslims. And quite a few Muslims chose to declare themselves as Yugoslavs, but we considered them to be Muslims because we claimed, as I said, on the basis of their first and last name and on the basis of their father's name, we claimed that they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, in 1991, when the census was taken, a Bosniak nationality did not exist.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone could declare himself or herself to be what he or she wanted to be. I can even remember that there was one person who declared himself to be an Eskimo. People were free to declare themselves as they liked in terms of nationality. And I can really remember that one person declared himself to be an Eskimo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But today, the people who declare themselves to be Bosniak in 1991, they would say that they were Muslims; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, why do you consider that people who declared themselves to be Yugoslav were in fact Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, because of their first and last name or because of -- either because of the surname or because of the first name, and also on the basis of the father's name. I would just like to add that if you look at this from the perspective of nationality, of the nationality of Muslims within the former Yugoslavia, and as far as I know, and I do know this, on the basis of what my parents claimed, my mother was not able to declare herself in national terms. She had to remain undeclared. But men were allowed to declare themselves. They would be either Serbs or Croats. But they could not declare themselves to be Muslims after the Second World War. As far as I remember, in 1974, the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina recognised the category of Muslims, recognised Muslims as a nationality, as they say. They recognised Muslims with a capital M. Up until then, women were not allowed to declare their nationality. They did not have this right. And when I say why people who declare themselves to be Yugoslavs, why we treated them as Muslims, I said on what basis this was done, and in historical terms, for a certain time, women were not allowed to declare themselves as being members of a certain nationality. It's the name which is indicative. Muslims have their own names. They don't have the names of other peoples. But these Yugoslavs were probably -- probably came from mixed marriages, and those who were communists or rather atheists, they would declare themselves as Yugoslavs, to be members of the Yugoslav people, although I know that this people was not even recognised in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There were Slovenes, Croats, Macedonians, Montenegrins, Muslims with a capital M, that was recognised in 1974, but there were no Yugoslavs. But since anyone was allowed to declare himself or herself to be a member of a certain nationality, this is what people did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I don't think I have understood you very well. Are you telling us that in Yugoslavia before 1974, women and men did not have the same rights, that women did not have civilian and political rights?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to say that I don't know up until when, but women who were Muslims, were not able to declare themselves as being members of a certain nationality. Therefore they had no rights either. They had to remain undeclared, undeclared. And when they were able to declare themselves as being members of a certain nationality, I cannot say exactly, but I think that the concept of a Muslim people, with a capital M, and reference in this case was made to the -- to what they declared themselves to be in terms of nationality rather than to religion. So a Muslim in this national sense, this idea was introduced I think, in 1974, perhaps even in 1971, when certain amendments were introduced. I can't state this exactly. But I do know that they weren't able to declare themselves as members of a given people. First of all, my mother and everyone else, they remained undeclared, because they couldn't state which nationality, which people, they belonged to, whereas men were not able to declare themselves to be Muslims but they were able to declare themselves as Serbs or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I'm now suggesting and objecting to this line. We are getting so far away from any point that is relevant to -- as far as I can see, General Talic's Defence. Your Honour, I accept that the witness gave a description of a number of Muslims. He's given his explanation. Madam Fauveau has, in our submission, cross-examined quite long enough about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau, what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, it's not pertinent to the Defence of General Talic, but it is a very important, as far as the witness's credibility is concerned. But I'm going to move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I said I appreciate that, thank you, Madam Fauveau. I thought it was on. It was off. I have a habit of switching it off sometimes or have it switched off, I don't know. Yes, please proceed. And Mr. Dzonlic, I noticed as we go along, I fully understand that you've been here for days at length, and this is tiring. I have noticed that your answers now tend to become longer and longer and longer, perhaps it's time for me to remind you of what I told you on the first day you arrived here. Please answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question, because you will -- that way, you will go back to your country quicker. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I promise that I'll finish today.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the mosque called Potpecinska Mosque was damaged in 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many mosques were there in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you left Banja Luka in February, 1993, had the Ferhadija Mosque been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Had the Arnaudija Mosque been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Had the Sefer Beg Mosque been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there Catholic church in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there just one or were there several?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the Catholic churches that you knew, had they been destroyed when you left Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that one -- one of them, whether it was a church or a Catholic monastery in the Paprikovac settlement, I heard that it had been set on fire while I was still down there, that was in 1992. And that another Catholic institution, in the direction of Laktasi, where there were sisters of a certain order, I heard that it had been destroyed too. I didn't see that but that's something that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you personally, did you personally see a Catholic church that had been destroyed or damaged in Banja Luka before you left?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't personally see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many orthodox churches there were in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were but there were several of them, three or four, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to the last series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this point, please choose whether you want to continue for the next five minutes or whether you prefer to stop now and resume after the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer to stop, I think it will take me another 15 minutes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All I want to know, is realistically, the next witness has actually been waiting since 10.00 this morning. Am I going to get him started? I know, Mr. Ackerman has another couple of matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the situation seems to be as follows: We stop at half 12.00. We resume roughly at just before 1.00. We have another 15 minutes to 20 minutes cross-examination. I don't know what Mr. Ackerman has for us. I don't know how long you expect to keep us engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think quite brief. Sometimes things get longer than I expect them to be but I think quite brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few questions in re-examination but only two or three, three or four, but I mean realistically is it worth keeping a witness in a rather unpleasant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, frankly, we can send the witness back to where he's staying because all we can get from him is the initial few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we have to go into closed session as well and that's another few minutes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. If we finish ten minutes earlier than we are expected to, it's not going to matter much. I think you can send the witness and we will resume at 1.00 or 5 to 1.00, and we will take it up from there. So. And then we will have the whole day of tomorrow. Incidentally there was some talk about the possibility of us sitting in the afternoon rather than in the morning tomorrow. It's not going to happen. The sitting is as scheduled at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So can we have the witness brought in, please? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, you said during the hearing of the 28th of February this year that during the third and last search that took place in your house, the people who were doing the search seized the permission that you had to leave Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you receive that document of permission to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you time wise when it was I received it. I don't remember. Maybe -- I don't know. Prior to them seizing that permit, I had received it, but when, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in order to obtain this permission, did you fulfil all the necessary formalities?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you went to the police to say that you were going to change your address?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you in fact intend to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I decided on the 20th of February, I think it was, anyway I left on the 26th but I decided to leave, to take that step, maybe ten or so days prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So when you had the permission to leave Banja Luka, you hadn't even decided to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had intended to go but I still hadn't decided definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And while telling the police that you no longer lived at the address at which you were living, you were able to remain in Banja Luka without any problem?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I deregistered very early on. As for all the other documents, I got hold of them much later. It was early on that I deregistered or reported the change of address in Banja Luka. And I remained there until the 26th of February. I think it was the 26th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment you informed the police that you were going to leave Banja Luka, you continued working in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did work.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So in a certain sense, you were in Banja Luka illegally, in a sense?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it illegally. I was in my own house. I was in Banja Luka. Now, whether that's illegal or legal. I wouldn't call it illegal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you changed your domicile, didn't you? You informed the police that you were changing your domicile?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me move on, then, to another question. Finally, when you left Banja Luka on the 26th of February, 1993, you said that you were prohibited from leaving the town. You said that during your previous testimony, on the 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the secretariat with my wife to see the chief or the secretary, I forget the full title. Anyway I know that his name was, I think, Denic, and he said to me, "I have received orders that your husband may not leave Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During that same hearing, you said, and it is page 2.490, the transcript in French, so there may be a difference in the page number, you said, "Here is the -- that is how I joined the convoy, but officially I was on the list for Novska but I left in a completely different direction and I entered our territory." Were you really telling us that what you were prohibited from doing was leaving for Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was not what I intended to say. What I meant was that I officially applied through the Municipal Red Cross. I handed in my documents in one direction, but to conceal my destination because I was very much afraid, then illegally, contrary to that list, I went in this other direction to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you disturbed because you were on the Red Cross list for Novska? Were you worried?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was worried. I was worried. This was maybe four or five days prior to my leaving for Travnik or maybe even two or three days prior to that, and I was -- I spent two nights at my aunt's. I didn't sleep in my own home because they took this permit and they said that I wasn't allowed to leave, and I was concerned. As far as I can remember, this was three or four days before -- anyway, a short while. And then I joined this other convoy. I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, would you agree with me if I were to suggest to you that the authorities of Republika Srpska would not let you go to Travnik but would let you go to Novska?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I wouldn't agree with you. They told me or rather this gentleman said to me, or rather my wife, "Your husband is not allowed to leave Banja Luka." That's what he said. And the fact that they took away this permit, my understanding was that I wasn't allowed to go anywhere, not just in one particular direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why were you on this Red Cross list for Novska?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I applied to the Red Cross to leave, believing that as this was the Red Cross, it was independent and unbiased, and I'd go through them because it was more difficult because I thought I couldn't leave through Perka's agency because all the lists were being checked and that is why I applied to the Red Cross, and I asked a friend of mine who used to be at the university with me, and her mother worked in the Municipal Red Cross to help me and to put me on this list, because I thought they wouldn't check the lists of the Municipal Red Cross. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So in spite of the prohibition, you went to the Red Cross and you asked to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And eventually, why did you change your direction?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I consulted my parents and we agreed that if possible, through Perka's agency, I could join the convoy without being on the list, I thought that would be safer for me, but if they were to be -- to trace me, then they would trace me through the Red Cross in Novska and it proved to be successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The people in this agency, did they know that you were on this convoy for Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother and my wife went to see Perka, as I said, through a colleague of my wife's, and they agreed with her, they gave her 500 Deutschmarks, and she said there would be no problems, that I should come on such and such a day, and I got on, and I assume that they knew that I was on this convoy. I arrived in the morning, I don't remember what time it was, and I got on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you trusted these people, you weren't afraid that they would denounce you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it trust. In those days at least, they would do anything for money, and that's what they did, and it was a risk, and they were ready to do anything for money. And I thought that this colleague of my wife's was related to Perka, I was just afraid of being on the list that would be sent to the police, and she said that she would not put me on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment ago you told us that you thought that it would be safer to leave through the Red Cross and now you're saying that they did anything for money. Why in that case did you not go directly to that agency?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you told me that you went to the Red Cross because you believed it was safer than the agency. Now you're telling me that it was possible to do anything with money in the agency. So in that case, why didn't you go directly to the agency?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to the agency. When this Perka told my mother and my wife that I wouldn't be on the list and that I could join the convoy, I decided to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: To close this subject, so one could say that this Madam Perka assisted you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, she did help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, would you agree with me that the authorities of Republika Srpska would not allow men of military age to go to Travnik because they would then be mobilised into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Very few able-bodied men, or that was the story in town, could go to Travnik, very few who were of military age could go to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you, you did indeed leave for Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were indeed mobilised to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the army for nine months.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no more questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So Ms. Korner, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, may I just understand the suggestion about the permission being denied to leave Banja Luka? Was the suggestion that he would have been allowed to leave Banja Luka if he'd put down Novska rather than Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so. That is the suggestion of the Defence. Re-examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I want to go back just over a couple of matters you were asked about. When you made your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in October, 1992, how clear were you on what months certain events happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always gave estimates. I was never sure about dates. In the course of this testimony, I realise that I made some errors regarding dates, so I was not certain. I was not sure about dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions about the meeting that was held to discuss the setting up of the Commission for Prisoners of War, to put it colloquially. It was put to you that in your statement you said that was about April, and you were asked about the attack on Kozarac. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you this: Which is clearer, that this meeting took place in April or that it took place after the attack had happened at Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was April but I'm not quite sure. I think I would be more certain of saying that it was in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: From your recollection now, was that meeting after the attack on Kozarac or are you unable to tell us?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to say. I know there was an attack. I know that there were events in Prijedor. But I cannot explicitly say whether it was before or after the attack on Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, one of the questions that you were asked by Mr. Ackerman related to your description of the procedures that had to be carried out in order for a person to leave Banja Luka. You remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And it was suggested that in effect, much the same regulations had existed before the Crisis Staff came into operation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: One of the matters that you said you had to do after the Crisis Staff was to sign a document saying that you were leaving Banja Luka voluntarily and for economic reasons. Was that something that had to be brought into --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't ask him about that. She's raising a new matter that was not covered on cross-examination. I think that's inappropriate. I didn't ask him anything about a document and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. signing a document about voluntarily departing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may not have asked him but he did mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He mentioned it on direct examination. I didn't ask any questions about it. She is just repeating some direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken. I think he is right. Unless you can prove that he did ask him the question. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was taken through -- if there is no suggestion, may I say, that this particular aspect, saying -- leaving voluntarily and for economic reasons existed before the Crisis Staff, then I certainly won't pursue it but as Your Honour appreciates because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand your point definitely. The only thing is that here and now, I don't remember whether he stated -- he made that affirmation as a result of a question from Mr. Ackerman or whether it was in response to a question from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. He gave that long description in the middle of which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman was -- and I stopped him actually at a certain point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the point is this, Your Honour: As Mr. Ackerman doesn't feel it's necessary to put his case properly, I don't know at the moment whether that particular part is contested, in other words, it's suggested that that also happened before the Crisis Staff or not. So I'm going back over that one part because that seems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand and I think I will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, that part of the procedure you described, did that exist before the advent of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked about releases that had taken place from the Manjaca camp at various periods of the year. Do you know anything about a visit made to Manjaca by a delegation led by a gentleman called Sir John Thompson?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of any combined Red Cross/European Community Monitoring Mission airlift from Manjaca in about September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about any such mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I want you to have a look again, please, at the document that you were shown of an order signed by General Talic, which has been marked DT2. Perhaps the witness could have the B/C/S copy and the English should be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The English is on the back side of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can have two copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do Your Honours have copies there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the copies we have are single-sided print. So it's no problem. But if we need them for the ELMO for the interpreters, do you have the document now? I'm addressing the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We don't seem to be able to locate it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not -- I'm simply going to break this up so my questions will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: First, Mr. Dzonlic, before were you shown this today, had you ever seen that order?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that on the 7th of June, 1992, General Talic had issued such an order to his troops?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise but I only have the document in English. Earlier, during the examination by the lady, I'm sorry, I've forgotten the name, I think that is the document that I had and there was point 3, when the lady told me to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I see what the witness has got? He hasn't got the B/C/S version. He's just got an English version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This was the document that was given to me during the break because I gave my copy to one of the judges and kept the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, hang on, I've got -- I'm sorry, I've got one here. There is a B/C/S version, Mr. Usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Dzonlic, I'll repeat the question. Were you aware that apparently on the 7th of June, General Talic had issued an order in these terms to his troops?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw Manjaca, how would you describe the accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a question that was already put to the witness during the examination in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Madam Fauveau is correct, is right. Could you rephrase it in some way which would be acceptable within the framework of a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw Manjaca, did that accord with the order that says that prisoners of war should be treated in a dignified way, humane way, without violence?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite the contrary. It was a -- it was contrary to this order. It was inhumane, it was -- there were lots of insults, there was lots of violence and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, and you had examined the Geneva Conventions, was the treatment of prisoners at Manjaca in accordance with the conventions or as described here with the provisions of international war law?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I object to that. That's the ultimate question that this Chamber must decide and this witness should not be asked to substitute his judgement for yours or to suggest what your judgement should be with regard to whether or not the treatment of prisoners at Manjaca was in accord with Geneva Conventions. That's your job. You have to decide that at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is definitely our job, Mr. Ackerman, but also the witness stated that he -- one of the roles that he was playing was to liaise with the Municipal Red Cross or International Red Cross and that part of the visit was intended to have a report prepared, which he did in fact prepare. So that would have covered also aspects under the Geneva Conventions. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Will I then be permitted to bring witnesses to give their opinions as to whether the Prosecution has proved a case against Mr. Brdjanin or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What kind of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just anybody, anybody who is familiar with the law, to come say, "I've looked at the evidence in the case Your Honours and I believe the Prosecution has failed to prove the case."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not what we mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's being asked is the treatment there in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. That is not his job. That's your job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't ask this question were it not for the fact that Mr. Dzonlic took with him the Geneva Conventions of which he made a study and indeed raised with Commander Popovic that this treatment was in breach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is why I'm allowing him -- I mean, the difference between any witnesses that you may refer to and Mr. Dzonlic is -- that Mr. Dzonlic went there with a specific purpose -- specific mission --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Further, may I finish? This document, may I say, was not put in by Mr. Ackerman and I'm not sure why Mr. Ackerman as opposed to Madam Fauveau is on his feet, but this document was put in by Madam Fauveau presumably to show that Talic had issued instructions that the camp should be in accordance with the provisions of international laws of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I seem to recall that I asked the witness some questions that had to do with the law and he was not permitted to answer them because he was not qualified as an expert on the law. I think the Judge said he's not qualified as an expert on the law and therefore he doesn't have to answer the question. Now, apparently, he's being treated as an expert on the law of the Geneva Conventions and international law and is now going to be permitted to give his opinion as an expert on this matter. And I think that's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- I don't want to waste time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will withdraw the question purely out of the interest of time and not because I accept Mr. Ackerman's objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Dzonlic, I want to ask you, please, to look at a document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was disclosed to the Defence on the 23rd of August of last year. It wasn't put in because I didn't appreciate that this point was going to be challenged. Would Your Honours -- I think I'm going to ask the witness to have the B/C/S copy and for the other copy to be put on the ELMO so that we can see the English version. I want the witness to deal with it, please, and then we will deal with the exhibits, I'm sorry, because we have to finish in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document, Mr. Dzonlic, that I don't think you saw at the time; is that correct? In other words, in February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, I think the first time you saw it was when you were here?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's dated the 2nd of February, 1993, "addressed to the Ministry of Defence Banja Luka district to the chief, Banja Luka subject request, in accordance with the agreement to control the issuance of permits for a change of residence, we found out that before the agreement, a permit to move away issued to Amir Dzonlic", and gives your parents' name, born on the 30th of October, 1959 in Banja Luka a lawyer, permanently residing in Banja Luka" and gives your address. "We therefore ask you to find a way to withdraw the permit and in future, refuse to issue this person a permit to change his place of residence or to leave the Republika Srpska on other grounds." And it's signed, "Chief of Sector Nedjeljko Kezic." Your Honour, he's one of the people who appears on the list of the Crisis Staff. Your Honour, technically this witness can't identify it, but as I say, it was disclosed. I can deal with where it comes from but I'd ask Your Honours to admit -- unless there is an objection, I'd ask Your Honours to admit that and make it Exhibit P--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there being no objection, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There being so objection and also because the document is definitely relevant, it's being admitted as Exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P473, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will insure that copies will be distributed. Thank you very much indeed, Mr. Dzonlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Dzonlic, that brings an end to your testimony here. I thank you. You may withdraw. We have a few minutes, I understand Mr. Ackerman -- you may withdraw. I thank you so much for being so patient and for having been with us to answer all these questions for one day after the other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to thank you and to express my deep respect. I would also like to take this opportunity to thank the Prosecution and the Defence for having conducted themselves in an appropriate, in a correct, manner during this hearing. And I wish good health to the accused and hope that they will be able to face the truth and justice in the best way possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may withdraw. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The only thing that I had to raise at this point, there are actually two matters. The first one is we were having a discussion earlier on in the testimony of this witness about the documents that he says were brought to him by clients which showed that they had been dismissed because of the order of the Crisis Staff. I want to have those documents produced. We stopped discussing it the other day because it was being done in his presence and we are now out of his presence and I think those are clearly the best evidence, and I think they are producable and should be produced. And so I would ask the Court to request or order the Prosecution to obtain those documents and make them available. And the other thing, Your Honour, I think Ms. Korner will talk about, has to do with this whole Rule 90(H) business and she and I have discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the first, I have no doubt that if Your Honours make an order, Mr. Dzonlic will comply with it. We can make arrangements for someone from the Sarajevo office to collect them from him. I repeat that our reluctance to take them was that, as I say, these are privileged documents, as far as we can see, but I don't think Mr. Dzonlic will raise an argument and we will provide copies. I don't think we can ask him to provide -- Mr. Dzonlic will, to our office, and we will pass them to the Defence, but I think Your Honours will have to make the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will think about it and we'll tell you what our decision will be. With regard to 90(H) do you have to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seemed, on reflection, having discussed the matter with Mr. Ackerman, the simplest way is we are going to put in a reply tomorrow to Mr. Ackerman's motion. We would then ask Your Honours to make as quick a ruling as is possible, simply indicating, if Your Honours are minded, to refuse Mr. Ackerman's motion what in your view it is meant by the putting of a case, and then if Mr. Ackerman still disputes it, or anybody does, he can go to the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do keep in mind one other important matter, whether the question of the conformity of the Rule with the Statute is a matter to be decided by the Trial Chamber or by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Your Honour, I don't think that matter is -- we are going to merely deal with his points on putting your case. We will be suggesting that Your Honours couldn't possibly decide that the Rule was in breach of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Until now I had kept my mouth closed on this matter but now that you are -- I think it's only fair that I do mention it to you without telling you what our position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour. I think there must be some kind of a concise ruling from which I can appeal. If there is no ruling, then there is nothing to appeal. And the other thing is, 73(C) seems to indicate, and of course it's totally up to Your Honours how you want to interpret it, it seems to indicate that the certification that it talks about -- the language is, "With seven days of the filing of the certification." So it appears that there must be a filing of the certification. And probably that certification must refer to a specific, concise ruling or decision so that the Appeals Chamber will have something to deal with when it gets to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very well. We'll see about that. Tomorrow morning we will resume at 9.00. I must inform you also that Friday, we will be sitting in the afternoon rather than in the morning. The reason is that the courtroom is needed for something else. Anyway, we have consulted -- we've been consulted and we have agreed to shift the sitting to the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that puts me in severe personal difficulties. Your Honour, I have a flight booked for London in the afternoon, and I anticipate that the witness coming tomorrow may still be going. Your Honour, I didn't know that. No advance warning was given, I'm afraid. All the I can ask is that Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I will take it in hand immediately and I will let you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will let you know. What time is your flight? If I may ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, I will deal with it. Yes, Madam Fauveau, you have problems, too?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have no problems, but I think I forgot something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I would prefer to be there but I'm staying here over the weekend. The only thing I wanted to ask you was for the documents DT2 and DT3 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I have the same request. On 46AB through 49AB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Granted. Tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
